title: Escape Velocity, Orbital Velocity and Satellites
subcategory: Gravitation — Escape Velocity, Satellites, Kepler's Laws

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — Gravitation

summary: Escape velocity is the minimum speed to permanently break free of a planet's gravity from its surface; orbital velocity is the (smaller) speed needed to maintain a stable circular orbit at a given height, and both follow from equating gravitational and kinetic/centripetal energy.
explanation: Escape velocity ve is found by setting the total mechanical energy at the surface to zero (just enough kinetic energy to reach infinity with zero leftover speed): ½mve² = GMm/R, giving ve = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR). For Earth, ve ≈ 11.2 km/s, independent of the escaping object's mass and independent of launch direction (ignoring atmospheric drag). Orbital velocity vo for a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r is found by equating gravitational force to the required centripetal force: GMm/r² = mvo²/r, giving vo = √(GM/r) = √(gR²/r); notice vo = ve/√2 at the same radius, so orbital speed is always less than escape speed. A geostationary satellite orbits with the same angular velocity as Earth's rotation (period = 24 h), appears fixed over one point on the equator, and must be at a specific altitude (~36,000 km) — this height is not adjustable independent of the period, since the two are linked by Kepler's third law. Kepler's three laws (elliptical orbits with the Sun/planet at one focus; equal areas swept in equal times, a consequence of angular momentum conservation; T² ∝ r³) describe all gravitationally bound orbits, not just planets around the Sun. Total energy of a satellite in a bound orbit is negative (E = −GMm/2r); a body with zero or positive total energy is not bound and will escape rather than orbit.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking escape velocity depends on the direction or angle of launch — for a given height it is a scalar minimum speed independent of direction (in the absence of air resistance).
Confusing escape velocity with orbital velocity, or assuming they're equal — orbital velocity is always ve/√2 at the same distance, noticeably smaller.

Believing any satellite placed above the equator becomes geostationary — geostationary status additionally requires the specific altitude that matches Earth's 24-hour rotation period, via Kepler's third law.
examples: A rocket needs ~11.2 km/s at Earth's surface to escape Earth's gravity completely, ignoring air resistance.
Communication satellites are placed in geostationary orbit so ground antennas can stay fixed, pointing at one spot in the sky.
genZNote: Escape velocity: the exact 'main character' speed you need to never look back at Earth.
